opus-5.5.text:
I think it's coming, but I'd be careful about what we mean by a "ChatGPT moment." For language, that moment was when ordinary people typed something in and suddenly felt the model understood them. It was general, it was accessible, and it worked well enough across many tasks that people immediately saw its value.

For Physical AI, the bar is different, and in some ways higher. A robot or an autonomous system doesn't just need to say something reasonable. It has to act in the real world, where mistakes have physical consequences. A chatbot can be wrong ninety-five percent of the way and still be useful. A robot that drops the cup five percent of the time, or bumps into a person, isn't something you'd put in your home.

So where are we? I'd say the foundations are being laid right now. A few things are converging. First, we have much better world models: systems that learn how the physical world evolves, how objects move, how actions lead to outcomes. That's a big part of what my team has been working on. Second, simulation and synthetic data are getting good enough to cover the long tail of situations you can't easily collect in reality. Third, the vision-language-action style models are showing that the same scaling recipe from language can transfer, at least partially, to embodied control.

The biggest bottleneck is still data. In language we had the internet: decades of text, essentially free. There's no internet of robot actions. Every demonstration has to be collected, on specific hardware, in specific environments. That's why I believe world models and simulation matter so much. They're our way of manufacturing the experience the internet gave language models for free.

My honest view is that the moment won't be one product launch. It'll come gradually, first in more structured settings like factories, warehouses, and driving, where the environment is somewhat controlled and the economic value is clear. Then, as the models generalize better, you'll see systems that can be put in a new place, given a new task, and just figure it out. When people see a robot do something it was never explicitly trained for, and do it reliably, that's when it will feel like a ChatGPT moment.

As for timing, I'm optimistic. The progress over the last two or three years has been much faster than I expected. But I'd rather say "within the next several years, in specific domains first" than promise a single dramatic date. Physics is less forgiving than language, and I think the field earns credibility by being honest about that.

r001.rationale: The response describes language AI’s broad success and says its scaling recipe can transfer to embodied control, identifying Digital AI as a foundation for Physical AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the ChatGPT moment for Physical AI is coming, but it will look different from the one we saw with language models, and I want to be honest about why.

The reason ChatGPT could happen when it did is that the internet handed us trillions of tokens of human-written text for free. Language is already a compressed, structured representation of how humans think, and it was sitting there waiting to be scraped. Physical AI has no equivalent. There is no internet of robot actions. Nobody has recorded billions of hours of a robot arm picking up a cup with the joint torques labeled. So the biggest bottleneck is not the architecture. The transformer works fine. The bottleneck is data.

That is why so much of our thinking goes into world foundation models and simulation. If you cannot collect the data, you have to generate it. A world model that understands physics, that can take a scene and roll forward what happens when you push, drop, or stack something, lets you produce enormous amounts of training experience that is cheap, diverse, and safe to collect. Real robot data remains the gold standard, and we still need it to ground everything, but synthetic data is how you get the scale that made language models work.

The second difference is the cost of being wrong. When a chatbot hallucinates, you get a wrong sentence. When a robot hallucinates, something breaks or someone gets hurt. So the bar for deployment is much higher, and the moment will arrive in stages rather than overnight. I expect we will first see generalist policies that transfer across tasks in controlled settings like warehouses and factories, then move toward less structured environments.

What makes me optimistic is that all the ingredients are converging at once. We have scalable pretraining recipes borrowed from language and vision. We have simulation that is getting photoreal and physically faithful. We have compute that keeps growing. And hardware, especially humanoids, has become good enough and cheap enough that many companies can experiment at once. When those lines cross, you get a surprising step function, the same way nobody predicted exactly when GPT-3 would become useful.

So my honest answer is that the moment is real and probably closer than most people think, maybe within a few years for narrow but genuinely general-purpose capability. But it will be earned through data engineering and simulation rather than a single clever model, and the first version will feel more like an extremely capable intern in a factory than a robot in your kitchen.

r001.rationale: The response presents language models’ success, including ChatGPT and GPT-3, as a source of scalable pretraining recipes that Physical AI can borrow and build on.

astra-6.text:
I think Physical AI can have a ChatGPT moment, but the question is what that moment will look like. Will it be a robot that can do one task extremely well, or a system that can adapt to many different tasks with very little additional training? To me, the second is the more meaningful milestone.

The challenge is that physical intelligence requires a whole loop: perception, reasoning, action, and then understanding how the world changed because of that action. And the cost of making a mistake can be much higher than generating an incorrect sentence.

Data is another key issue. For language, we had an enormous amount of text available to learn from. For physical interaction, we need examples of actions and their consequences across many environments. Simulation could be very important here, because it gives us a way to generate experience and test systems, although transferring that learning into the real world remains a challenge.

So I’m optimistic about the direction, but cautious about predicting a date. The moment I would look for is when someone can give a robot a new task in ordinary language, and it can carry it out reliably in an unfamiliar environment. That would be a very compelling demonstration of generalization.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts language’s large text corpus with the data needs of physical interaction, but does not identify Digital AI’s success as a foundation for Physical AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Physical AI has tremendous potential, but its ChatGPT moment may look different. With language, you can train on enormous amounts of text and evaluate a response almost immediately. In the physical world, an action has consequences, and collecting diverse, useful experience is much harder.

The key question is whether we can build models that generalize across tasks and environments, rather than learning one narrowly defined behavior. Simulation and world models could help by giving these systems a way to learn from many more situations than we can practically collect in the real world. But the transfer back to reality has to work reliably.

So I’m optimistic about the direction, but cautious about predicting a date. For me, the moment will be when you can give a robot a new task in an unfamiliar environment, and it can figure out what to do without extensive task-specific engineering. A compelling demonstration is a milestone; making that capability dependable and broadly useful is the bigger challenge.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts language AI’s training and evaluation advantages with physical-world challenges, but does not identify Digital AI’s success as a foundation for Physical AI to build on.
